title: Range Sum Query — Immutable
statement: Design a class NumArray that is constructed from an integer array which never changes afterwards, and supports sumRange(left, right) returning the sum of nums[left..right] inclusive. sumRange will be called many times — many more times than the constructor.
realWorld: A dashboard where the user drags a time window across a fixed day of metrics: the series is loaded once and never changes, but the window moves on every mouse event. What matters is the per-query cost, not the load cost, and that trade — pay once at construction, answer instantly forever after — is the same one an index makes in a database.

examples.explanation: -2+0+3 = 1; 3-5+2-1 = -1; the whole array sums to -3. The three ranges overlap heavily, which is exactly the redundancy worth eliminating.
A range of one element must return that element, and a range covering everything must return the total — the two ends of the index arithmetic, and where off-by-one bugs show up first.
The smallest possible instance. It only works if the prefix array has a leading zero, so that prefix[1] - prefix[0] is defined.

constraints: Up to 10^4 calls to sumRange, and the array is never modified

bruteForce.whySlow: Two queries that overlap re-add every element they share, and consecutive window positions in a dashboard overlap in all but one element. Nothing at all carries from one call to the next, so a query covering half a 10,000-element array re-adds the same 5,000 numbers that the previous query just finished adding — 10^4 queries over a static array perform up to 10^8 additions, all of them recomputing sums of a sequence that by assumption never changes.

patternIdentification: The data is immutable and the same aggregate is asked repeatedly over different ranges: that is the signal to move work from query time to construction time. Any range aggregate whose operator has an inverse — sum with subtraction, XOR with itself — collapses into a single precomputed array of prefixes plus one combine per query. If the array were mutable this trade would break down and the answer would be a Fenwick or segment tree, which buys O(log n) updates at the cost of O(log n) queries.

optimized.idea: In the constructor, build prefix[i] = the sum of the first i elements, in an array one slot longer than the input so that prefix[0] = 0 stands for the empty prefix. Then the sum of nums[left..right] is prefix[right + 1] - prefix[left]: everything up to the end of the range, minus everything before it starts. Construction costs one pass; every query afterwards is a single subtraction, independent of how wide the range is. The leading zero is not decoration — it is what makes a range starting at index 0 need no special case.
code: prefix = new int[nums.length + 1];          // one longer, and prefix[0] stays 0
public int sumRange(int left, int right) {
return prefix[right + 1] - prefix[left];    // one subtraction, whatever the width

commonMistakes: Sizing the prefix array at n and defining prefix[i] as the sum of nums[0..i]: every query then needs left == 0 ? prefix[right] : prefix[right] - prefix[left - 1], and the branch that is forgotten sends prefix[-1] into an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException on the first query that starts at index 0.

Writing prefix[right] - prefix[left] with the exclusive convention: every answer is short by exactly nums[right], which is invisible whenever that element happens to be 0 and wrong everywhere else — sumRange(0,2) on [-2,0,3,-5,2,-1] returns -2 instead of 1.

Accumulating into an int when the constraints are larger than stated: 10^4 elements of magnitude 10^5 reach 10^9, one order of magnitude from wrapping, and an overflowed prefix shows up as a query over positive values returning a large negative number. A long[] prefix costs 8n bytes and removes the whole class of bug.

practice.note: LeetCode 303 is the immutable version taught here. 307 (Range Sum Query - Mutable) is the same question once updates are allowed, and needs a Fenwick or segment tree.
